title: Understanding grief and loss
citation: Shear, M. K. (2015). Complicated grief. New England Journal of Medicine, 372(2), 153-160.
content:
Understanding grief and loss.

Grief is the natural emotional, psychological, and physical response to losing someone or something important. Although it is most commonly associated with the death of a loved one, grief can also follow other significant losses, such as the end of a relationship, changes in health, losing a job, or major life transitions. Grief is not something to be fixed. It is a process of adapting to life after a meaningful loss, and everyone experiences it differently.

Shouldn't I be "over it" by now?

Many people worry that they are grieving for too long or not coping well enough. In reality, there is no universal timeline for grief. The intensity often changes over time, but the loss itself may always remain meaningful. Feeling sadness months or even years later does not necessarily mean something is wrong. It reflects the importance of what or who has been lost, rather than a failure to move on.

Why does grief feel so difficult?

Grief affects many parts of the brain and body because it involves adjusting to a world that has changed. Alongside emotional pain, people may notice difficulty concentrating, changes in sleep, fatigue, loss of appetite, or feeling physically exhausted. The brain is working to make sense of a significant change while also adapting to a new reality. That is why grief can feel overwhelming even when nothing appears physically wrong.

What grief can feel like and the different ways it shows up.

Grief does not look the same for everyone. Some people experience intense sadness, while others feel numb, angry, guilty, anxious, or even relieved, depending on the circumstances of the loss. Emotions can change from one day to the next, and many people notice that memories, anniversaries, places, or unexpected reminders can bring strong feelings back. There is no right way to grieve, and different emotional responses are all part of the normal grieving process.

Grief vs depression: what's the difference?

Grief and depression can share some experiences, such as sadness, reduced energy, changes in sleep, and difficulty concentrating, but they are not the same. Grief is usually connected to a specific loss, and although painful, positive memories and moments of connection or enjoyment can still occur alongside the sadness. Depression tends to affect mood, motivation, and enjoyment more broadly across many areas of life and may not be linked to one particular event. Understanding this difference can help people recognise that grief is a normal response to loss and not something that always indicates a mental health condition.

Why does grief come in waves instead of a straight line?

Grief rarely follows a predictable path. Many people describe it as coming in waves, where difficult emotions lessen for a while before returning unexpectedly. This happens because the brain continues to process the significance of the loss over time, and reminders such as anniversaries, familiar places, or important life events can temporarily reactivate feelings of grief. Moving between more difficult and easier days is a normal part of adapting to loss.

When does grief need professional support?

Grief is a natural response to loss, and most people gradually adapt with time and support from those around them. However, it can be helpful to speak with a mental health professional if grief continues to feel overwhelming, makes it difficult to manage everyday responsibilities, or leaves you feeling unable to adjust to life after the loss. Professional support can provide a safe space to process emotions, develop coping strategies, and help you adapt while continuing to honour the significance of what has been lost.
